title: Writing Game Stories That Survive Player Choice
authorship: Independent channel script; concept research only; no reference transcript translation or reuse

scenes.title: Players Choose the Reading Order
lines: A film presents its scenes in an edited order. In a game, even the first person you speak to can be your choice.
The official Divinity: Original Sin 2 footage shows several answers during a conversation. Good sentences alone do not define what happens after each choice.
In the authoring tool, a question and its action options are edited separately. This shows event construction, rather than proving every condition in the finished game.
We built a small story game called The Harbor Seal to test the problem. From this point, this screen is our own playable prototype.
Going straight to the harbor guard means we have neither the item nor the information yet. His first response must start from that state.
This time we read the notice first and come back. The place and character are unchanged, but the facts the player brings are different.
The next line should check what is true now before assuming a scene number. Let us draw that distinction.

scenes.title: Separate Scene Order from World State
lines: The first principle is to write order and state separately. Meeting the guard second does not mean the player knows the clue.
The script on the left lists scene one and scene two. The one on the right checks whether the clue was seen, the item is held, and the companion is present.
This does not require a new story for every combination. Write only the conditions needed for this particular line to be true.
For example, an uninformed player asks a question. An informed player can answer using the clue. The character can keep the same voice and goal.
Keep the condition for entering a scene separate from the condition for choosing a line. Combining them can make a small edit change an unexpected branch.

scenes.title: Player Knowledge Is Not Character Knowledge
lines: In this official Divinity conversation, the speaker addresses the protagonist by name. What we can observe is that recognition is expressed in the dialogue.
This short clip cannot establish how the recognition condition is implemented. We test who actually receives the information in our own game.
The notice explains the rule for proving passage. Reading it does not automatically tell the guard that the player has visited it.
We choose the answer that mentions the rule. That action records the information shared with the guard.
Talking again now continues the earlier conversation instead of asking the introductory question. Reading and sharing were implemented as different events.
We also try reading the record before meeting the guard. Whatever the visit order, a character should not pretend to know an unshared fact.
When a line sounds wrong, trace when that character learned the fact before rewriting the sentence.

scenes.title: Track Knowledge for Each Participant
lines: The second principle is to distinguish the owner of information. A world event, a fact seen by the player, and a fact shared with another character are separate records.
Three separate columns expose mistakes. A locked door is a world state. Reading why it was locked is player knowledge.
Only telling the guard makes it shared information. Until then, a line such as I know you read the notice would need another explanation.
Start with small facts needed by the dialogue: knowing a name, hearing a promise, or asking a question before. There is no need to record every irrelevant action.
On repeat conversations, retire answered questions and keep the replies that still make sense. Smooth writing is built on those conditions.

scenes.title: Check the Actual Owner of a Story Item
lines: The official Divinity authoring demonstration creates a ring, changes its name and description, and puts it into an inventory.
This is actual tool work preparing an item for a story. We do not invent a later plot consequence that this footage does not show.
In our harbor test, a companion can hold the seal. An item being somewhere in the party is different from the protagonist being able to present it now.
We pass the seal to the companion and speak with the guard. While the companion is present, an answer lets that companion show it.
This time we let the companion rest and return alone. A line claiming the protagonist takes the seal from a pocket would contradict its current owner.
The test checks the owner again, removes that answer, and keeps a way to recover the seal. We continue by meeting the companion and taking it back.
When turning prose into game dialogue, remember that held it, handed it over, and came together all require an actual state.

scenes.title: Past Acquisition Is Not Current Possession
lines: The third principle is to distinguish historical facts from current facts. Having acquired the seal earlier does not establish its current owner.
In the diagram, the item moves between the protagonist, companion, and storage. Its acquisition remains in history while its owner and location change.
Write which fact a line requires. Remembering an earlier discovery needs history. Offering to show the item now needs present ownership and access.
If a character can leave, inspect essential information and items held only by that character. Provide a fitting alternative source or recovery path.
Rather than removing freedom to prevent every exception, check that permitted changes are reflected consistently in later words and actions.

scenes.title: Keep Consequences When Branches Rejoin
lines: An event card in the Divinity authoring demonstration lists distinct actions such as attacking a wolf, feeding it, and running away.
Different labels do not automatically produce different consequences. The visible editing operation and the design of its outcomes must be considered separately.
Our own game gives three answers on the road to the harbor: give food, take a detour, or calmly drive the animal away.
Giving food uses a ration. Taking the detour takes more time. All three can reach the harbor, while resources and recorded events remain different.
We run the feeding route, then start a fresh run for the detour. A later line mentioning the journey changes to match the result.
Instead of building three enormous maps, the branches rejoin the same scene while carrying traces of their choices.
The question is whether the next statement about what this person did agrees with their actual action.

scenes.title: Rejoining Does Not Mean Forgetting
lines: The fourth principle is to define both common conditions and retained differences when branches rejoin. Reaching the harbor is shared.
Whether food was used or a detour taken can remain recorded. Even within the same scene, a short response or available answer can differ.
A line celebrating a victory requires that victory to have happened. A triumphant sentence after a failed encounter breaks the connection.
Winning and reaching the next area may be different facts. If defeat leads to rescue and continued progress, write lines for that route.
The goal is not to maximize the branch count. It is to keep the later story from contradicting an action the game allowed.

scenes.title: Make Essential Story Facts Recoverable
lines: The Divinity authoring tools prepare map locations and event cards separately. Seeing a location and hearing its explanation can be treated as separate facts.
In our test, we skip the opening explanation and go straight to the harbor. The immediate action should still be understandable without reading the long background.
The guard asks for a seal he has not received. The conversation still explains what is needed and where it can be checked.
Opening the notice lets the player recover the facts needed at this stage. The game does not force an answer that assumes unfamiliar history.
We also run the route that read the explanation. Previously heard material is not repeated; a short answer confirms the next action.
This is not a license to insert arbitrary exposition. The setting must explain why this place and character can provide that information.
Recoverable essential facts and optional background give each line a clearer purpose.

scenes.title: Separate Essential Facts from Background
lines: We now distinguish facts required for progress from background that adds richness. We classify their role, not just their length.
The condition for entering the harbor is essential. An incident from the guard’s childhood may be optional background.
If an essential fact exists only in a one-time scene, skipping that scene can erase the reason for the next action. Provide a natural way to check it again.
There is no need to repeat everything to a player who read it. Offer a brief confirmation to informed players and the necessary explanation to others.
This concerns missing or reordered story information during play: keeping a valid basis for dialogue throughout the narrative.

scenes.title: Test the Story in Different Orders
lines: We now change the dialogue conditions directly in our own story game. Finishing the normal route once can miss important combinations.
In the first run, we read the notice, acquire the seal, and meet the guard. Handing over the required item opens the next scene.
In the second run, we skip the explanation and meet the guard first. We check that the dialogue does not claim unlearned knowledge and that information remains accessible.
In the third run, we leave the seal with a resting companion. We compare the unavailable answer with its return after retrieving the item.
In the fourth run, we make different road choices. We check that rejoining the harbor does not overwrite rations or the journey record.
Each run records the action, changed facts, and selected dialogue together. When something fails, the connection can be traced in that record.
This test does not judge story enjoyment in place of people. It is a small technical check for contradictions between writing and actual play.

scenes.title: A Playable Script Includes Its Conditions
lines: A game script needs both its sentences and the conditions that make them valid. Record who knows what, who holds what, and which actions occurred.
Separate order from state and distinguish who owns information. Do not confuse past acquisition with present possession.
Keep traces of actions when branches rejoin, and let players recover essential facts they missed.
Finally, play through different orders and ownership states. Logs help locate contradictions; human play review evaluates understanding and emotion.
Add one line beside the dialogue you are writing: what must happen first for this statement to be true? That question connects game writing to actual play.
